title: The Ozone Hole (and Its Recovery)
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: A giant hole spotted above Antarctica, a treaty signed by 197 countries, and a planet that heals. Here is **the only great ecological crisis** that humanity has already solved.

hero.hook: A hole in the sky, discovered by chance, and closed by a treaty signed by the whole world.

blocks.text: In 1985, British scientists stationed in Antarctica could not believe their measurements: part of the sky seemed to have lost its protection against the Sun. It was not a device error, but a real hole in the ozone layer, this invisible shield that protects us all. This course tells the story of how the world discovered this danger and, unusually, how it managed to fix it.

sections.title: A fragile shield, a handy poison

blocks.text: The **ozone layer** is located between 15 and 35 kilometers above sea level, in the , and absorbs most of the **UV-B**, these rays from the Sun powerful enough to damage our skin and the DNA of living cells. In the 1930s, the industry invented **chlorofluorocarbons**, or : gases considered perfect, inexpensive, which were put everywhere, in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol cans. [[Stratosphere]] [[Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)]]

The problem is that these gases are too stable: instead of degrading near the ground, they rise to the stratosphere. In 1974, chemists Mario Molina and Frank Sherwood Rowland warned: under the influence of the Sun, CFCs release chlorine, which destroys ozone. They received the Nobel Prize in 1995, but almost no one listened to them then.

sections.title: 1985: the shock, then the global agreement

blocks.text: In 1985, the British Antarctic Survey confirmed the news: every spring, a spectacular hole opens in the ozone layer above . NASA satellites already had this data, but their software had dismissed it as too extreme to be true. [[Antarctica]]

blocks.caption: The ozone hole above Antarctica, seen by satellite.

blocks.text: The threat to human health is taken very seriously, and the world is responding quickly. In 1987, countries signed the , a treaty which organized the gradual phasing out of CFCs. It only has 24 countries at the start; today, it brings together **197**, all the members of the United Nations. [[The Montreal Protocol (1987)]]
The Montreal Protocol is the only treaty in the history of the United Nations ratified by every country in the world, without exception.

This success is due to a clear rule for all and a common fund helping poor countries to change their machines. Even manufacturers, initially against it, ended up following suit by finding profitable replacement products.

This success is often cited to say that we could solve climate change in the same way. But the two problems differ: the ozone hole came from a small number of gases produced by a small number of factories, which were easy to target.  comes out of almost everything our modern society does, moving, heating, cultivating, building: reducing CO₂ requires changing the entire global economy, not just a handful of chemical factories. [[Carbon dioxide (CO₂)]]
Good news by the way: CFCs were also powerful greenhouse gases. By banning them, the Montreal Protocol also slowed global warming, without that being its primary goal.
Without this treaty, CFCs could have added about 1°C of additional warming to the Earth by 2050, just because of their greenhouse effect.

sections.title: A slow but very real recovery

blocks.text: Chlorine already rising in the atmosphere takes time to disappear: it was not until the mid-1990s that levels of harmful gases stabilized. Since the early 2000s, the healing has been clear and measurable.

events.title: Return to normal (planned)
events.detail: The ozone layer should return to its 1980 level.

blocks.text: If the treaty continues to be respected, the ozone layer should return to its 1980 state by **2065-2070**, preventing millions of skin cancers and cataracts. We must remain vigilant: clandestine emissions of CFCs were spotted in East Asia a few years ago, proof that a global agreement only works if it is constantly monitored.
The ozone hole remains the only major environmental crisis entirely resolved by global cooperation: a treaty signed in 1987 by 197 countries, with scientifically measurable results.
